fire: Spain's inflation figures surprised analysts again this autumn. The national statistics office reported that consumer prices rose 3.4 percent in the year to September, driven largely by electricity bills and fresh food. Rents in Madrid and Barcelona climbed sharply, and economists at several banks raised their forecasts for the final quarter. Tourism-heavy regions such as the Balearic Islands saw some of the steepest increases. The central bank warned that wage settlements, many of them indexed to past inflation, could keep price growth elevated well into next year. Retailers said shoppers were switching to own-brand goods, delaying large purchases and cutting back on restaurant meals. In contrast, Portugal's annual rate was just 2.1 percent in September, held down by falling fuel costs and a cooling housing market.

Marcus Hale has been the revelation of the season at Ashford Town. Signed for a modest fee from a second-tier club last summer, the 24-year-old striker has adapted quickly to the manager's high-pressing system. He leads the line with energy, drops deep to link play, and has become the first name on the team sheet. Supporters have taken to singing his name before kick-off, and scouts from two Premier League sides were in the stands last weekend. Hale himself credits extra finishing sessions after training with the club's analysts. Whereas Hale has 14 league goals from 31 shots on target, his strike partner Diego Ruiz has managed only four from 29, and he was left on the bench for the derby.

The original Harbor Lights was a small film that became a quiet phenomenon. Shot in 23 days on a shoestring budget, it followed two estranged sisters running their late father's fishing boat off the coast of Maine. Director Anna Kessler let scenes breathe, trusting long silences and the grey Atlantic light to do the emotional work. The performances felt lived-in, the script avoided easy resolutions, and the final scene on the harbor wall still lingers years later. Critics championed it, and word of mouth kept it in cinemas for months. The same cannot be said for the sequel, which is louder, longer and oddly hollow, though that is not to say it lacks the occasional fine moment.

Humpback whales in the North Pacific undertake one of the longest migrations of any mammal. Each winter they leave feeding grounds off Alaska and travel thousands of kilometres to the warm, shallow waters around Hawaii and Mexico. There the males sing long, complex songs, and females give birth to calves that will make the return journey within a few months. During the breeding season the adults barely feed, living off fat reserves built up over the summer. Researchers track individuals by the unique black-and-white patterns on the underside of their tail flukes. Humpbacks in the Arabian Sea, on the other hand, never migrate at all, staying in their tropical waters year-round.

Engineers at a Swiss start-up say they have built a sodium-ion battery that could transform home energy storage. The cell uses abundant sodium in place of lithium and a cathode made from iron and manganese, avoiding cobalt entirely. In laboratory tests it retained 90 percent of its capacity after 5,000 full charge cycles, equivalent to well over a decade of daily use. The team says the cells are also safer, resisting thermal runaway even when punctured. A pilot production line is due to open next year near Basel, according to the company. The work was published this month in the journal Joule. Compared with the new design, the lithium-ion packs in most home systems typically fall to 80 percent capacity after about 3,000 cycles.

Athens built much of its power on silver. From the mines at Laurion, slaves extracted ore that was smelted and struck into the famous owl tetradrachms, coins stamped with the head of Athena on one face and her owl on the reverse. These coins circulated across the Mediterranean, from Sicily to Egypt, and were trusted for their consistent weight and purity. Even today, hoards of them turn up in excavations far from Attica. The silver also paid for the fleet of triremes that defeated Persia at Salamis in 480 BC. Athenian officials guarded the coinage closely and punished forgers severely. Unlike Athens, Sparta never minted its own silver coinage, relying instead on heavy iron bars that were almost useless for trade abroad.

Italy's economy delivered a pleasant surprise in the second quarter. Output rose 0.6 percent on the previous three months, according to the national statistics agency, the strongest reading in two years. Tourism provided a large lift, with record numbers of foreign visitors in Rome, Florence and along the Amalfi coast. Construction also held up well, helped by funds from the European recovery programme, and factory orders picked up in the industrial north. Household spending rose for a third straight quarter as employment reached a record high. Ministers in Rome welcomed the figures as evidence that recent reforms were bearing fruit. Germany and France, by comparison, grew 0.1 and 0.3 percent respectively over the same period.

The snake plant has earned its reputation as the easiest houseplant you can buy. Its stiff, upright leaves store water, so it can go three or four weeks without a drink, and it copes with dim corners, dry central heating and the occasional cold draught. It rarely suffers from pests, and repotting is needed only every few years, when the roots start to crack the pot. Many growers say the surest way to kill one is to love it too much, since overwatering quickly rots the base. While the snake plant shrugs off neglect, the fiddle-leaf fig is notoriously fussy, dropping its leaves after a single missed watering or a move to a new spot.
